beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. Imagine flying a commercial jet with no altimeter, no airspeed, no fuel gauge — just a text log that prints engine failed, after you have already hit the ground. That is an A.I. microservice without observability. Today: telemetry, time-series metrics, and how engineers keep a production system visible while it is still flying.

props.command: My service has been degrading for six days. What would have told me on day one?
output: error logs: clean — it never crashed

beats.honesty_note: The six-day scenario is illustrative of the silent-degradation failure the script describes. No incident is being reported.

beats.narration_text: Logs tell you why you crashed. Metrics tell you that you are descending — which is the only one of those two you can still act on, and the reason this is worth twelve minutes of setup.

props.text:
Logs are enough.
They only speak after the crash.

beats.authoring_note: Both readings are true sentences: 'Logs explain the crash.' and, corrected, 'Metrics explain the crash.' — the second is also true, and the pairing with 'only one prevents it' is what makes the swap land.

beats.narration_text: Observability rests on three pillars, and they are peers — not stages of a pipeline. Logs record what happened at one moment: a single error, with its stack trace. Traces follow one request as it hops between services, so you can see which hop was slow. Metrics are numbers sampled over time — latency, errors per second, cache hit ratio. You need all three, and they answer different questions.

beats.authoring_note: connectors:false — the script draws three PILLARS, not a pipeline. Connectors would assert that logs feed traces feed metrics, which is false and is exactly the misconception the beat is correcting.

beats.narration_text: A general-purpose relational database is a poor fit for millions of rapid measurements. Time-series databases, like the one inside Prometheus, store every point as a timestamp, a value, and a set of labels — and that changes the question you are able to ask. A row store answers what happened to user forty-two. A time-series store answers whether the ninety-ninth percentile latency tripled in the last ten minutes, which is the question that actually wakes somebody up.

props.stampSub: the storage model decides which questions are affordable

beats.honesty_note: The script says SQL databases are 'terrible' at this. Scoped to the real mechanism: a row store CAN hold the data, but it is indexed for identity rather than for ranges over time, so the aggregate queries cost far more. The 2M writes/hour figure is illustrative.

beats.narration_text: This is where it matters most for A.I. A model rarely fails with a five hundred error. It degrades quietly — it drifts, it gets more confident about things that are not true, and every request still returns two hundred O.K. So you track domain metrics, not just system ones: cache hit ratio, refusal rate, and how often your own guardrail is intercepting something. A rate that was flat at two percent for a month and is now at eighteen is a story your error log will never tell you.

beats.narration_text: So where does this break? A flat line is ambiguous. It means the system is healthy, or it means the thing that reports the number stopped reporting. Those render identically — and the second one looks more reassuring, because a dead collector produces no spikes at all. The fix is unglamorous: alert on the absence of data, not only on bad data. And be careful what you label, because a label with one value per user turns a time-series database into millions of separate series and takes the monitoring down with it.

props.leftText:
service A   2.0  2.0  2.0  2.0
service B   2.0  2.0  2.0  2.0

# A is fine.
# B stopped scraping on Tuesday.
props.hotNote: a dead collector never spikes — it looks like your calmest service
props.code:
- alert: TargetDown
  expr: up == 0
  for: 2m

- alert: NoFreshSamples
  expr: time() -
    timestamp(intercept_rate) > 300

# and keep labels low-cardinality:
# never label by user_id.
props.stampSub: monitor the monitoring, or the outage you miss is your own

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED. The script presents metrics as the early-warning system and never asks what happens when the warning system itself fails. Two failures are named: no-data rendering as good news, and cardinality explosion from per-user labels — the most common way teams take down their own Prometheus.

beats.narration_text: So instrument your blind spots. Pick the three numbers that would have told you something was wrong last time, emit them, and then write the alert that fires when they stop arriving at all.

props.title: metrics.py
props.code:
INTERCEPTS = Counter(
    "guardrail_intercepts_total",
    "claims blocked",
    ["reason"],          # low cardinality
)                        # never ["user_id"]

LATENCY = Histogram(
    "verify_seconds", "end-to-end verify"
)

# TASK: instrument your blind spots.

# Then alert on up == 0.
# A dead exporter is an outage.
props.sparkLine: Count what would have warned you.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own service. Ask a model which of your dashboards would look completely normal if the service stopped emitting metrics entirely. Whatever it lists is a panel that cannot tell you apart from a corpse.
